claim: Recent advances in functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) have helped elucidate previously inaccessible trajectories of early-life prenatal and neonatal brain development.
source: Recent advances in functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) have helped elucidate previously inaccessible trajectories of early-life prenatal and neonatal brain development.
evidence: This is a general statement about the field supported by the context of the manuscript and established scientific knowledge.

claim: To date, the interpretation of fetal–neonatal fMRI data has relied on linear analytic models, akin to adult neuroimaging data.
source: To date, the interpretation of fetal–neonatal fMRI data has relied on linear analytic models, akin to adult neuroimaging data.
evidence: This statement describes the current state of the field as presented in the manuscript.

claim: The fetal and newborn brain develops extraordinarily rapidly, far outpacing any other brain development period across the life span.
source: However, unlike the adult brain, the fetal and newborn brain develops extraordinarily rapidly, far outpacing any other brain development period across the life span.
evidence: This is supported by established scientific knowledge about brain development.

claim: Conventional linear computational models may not adequately capture accelerated and complex neurodevelopmental trajectories during the fetal-neonatal period.
source: Consequently, conventional linear computational models may not adequately capture these accelerated and complex neurodevelopmental trajectories during this critical period of brain development along the prenatal-neonatal continuum.
evidence: This is a hypothesis/speculation that motivates the study.

claim: The study developed quantitative, systems-wide representations of brain activity in a large sample (>500) of fetuses, preterm, and full-term neonates using a variational autoencoder (VAE).
source: To obtain a nuanced understanding of fetal–neonatal brain development, including nonlinear growth, for the first time, we developed quantitative, systems-wide representations of brain activity in a large sample (>500) of fetuses, preterm, and full-term neonates using an unsupervised deep generative model called variational autoencoder (VAE), a model previously shown to be superior to linear models in representing complex resting-state data in healthy adults.
evidence: This describes the methodology and sample size used in the study.

claim: VAE has been previously shown to be superior to linear models in representing complex resting-state data in healthy adults.
source: To obtain a nuanced understanding of fetal–neonatal brain development, including nonlinear growth, for the first time, we developed quantitative, systems-wide representations of brain activity in a large sample (>500) of fetuses, preterm, and full-term neonates using an unsupervised deep generative model called variational autoencoder (VAE), a model previously shown to be superior to linear models in representing complex resting-state data in healthy adults.
evidence: This references prior work on VAE models in adults.

claim: Nonlinear brain features (latent variables) derived with the VAE pretrained on rsfMRI of human adults carried important individual neural signatures.
source: Here, we demonstrated that nonlinear brain features, that is, latent variables, derived with the VAE pretrained on rsfMRI of human adults, carried important individual neural signatures, leading to improved representation of prenatal-neonatal brain maturational patterns and more accurate and stable age prediction in the neonate cohort compared to linear models.
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by the data presented.

claim: VAE-derived latent variables led to improved representation of prenatal-neonatal brain maturational patterns compared to linear models.
source: Here, we demonstrated that nonlinear brain features, that is, latent variables, derived with the VAE pretrained on rsfMRI of human adults, carried important individual neural signatures, leading to improved representation of prenatal-neonatal brain maturational patterns and more accurate and stable age prediction in the neonate cohort compared to linear models.
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by reconstruction performance data.

claim: VAE-derived latent variables led to more accurate and stable age prediction in the neonate cohort compared to linear models.
source: Here, we demonstrated that nonlinear brain features, that is, latent variables, derived with the VAE pretrained on rsfMRI of human adults, carried important individual neural signatures, leading to improved representation of prenatal-neonatal brain maturational patterns and more accurate and stable age prediction in the neonate cohort compared to linear models.
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by age prediction performance data in Tables 1-3.

claim: Using the VAE decoder, the study revealed distinct functional brain networks spanning the sensory and default mode networks.
source: Using the VAE decoder, we also revealed distinct functional brain networks spanning the sensory and default mode networks.
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by the network mapping results in Figure 7.

claim: In utero fetal brain development follows a highly organized, dynamic, and precisely patterned process that lays a critical foundation for lifelong neurodevelopmental and neuropsychiatric brain health.
source: In utero fetal brain development follows a highly organized, dynamic, and precisely patterned process that lays a critical foundation for lifelong neurodevelopmental and neuropsychiatric brain health (Amgalan et al., 2021; De Asis-Cruz et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The architecture of the human connectome changes rapidly with brain maturation and plays a critical role in critical periods of early brain development.
source: The architecture of the human connectome also changes rapidly with brain maturation and plays a critical role in critical periods of early brain development (De Asis-Cruz et al., 2021b; De Asis-Cruz et al., 2021a; Gilmore et al., 2018; Cao et al., 2017b).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) has become a powerful neuroimaging tool for investigating whole brain dynamics.
source: Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) has become a powerful neuroimaging tool for investigating whole brain dynamics (Fox and Raichle, 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The mature human brain is comprised of several overlapping large-scale brain networks subserving different sensorimotor and higher cognitive functions.
source: Seminal fMRI studies have shown that the mature human brain is comprised of several overlapping large-scale brain networks subserving different sensorimotor and higher cognitive functions (Damoiseaux et al., 2006; Buckner et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Functional brain networks (FBNs) evolve over the life span, from infancy to old age.
source: These functional brain networks (FBNs) evolve over the life span, from infancy to old age (Vij et al., 2018; Hu et al., 2022; Gao et al., 2009; Gao et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Sensorimotor networks have been shown to develop around the third trimester of pregnancy ~30 wk.
source: Sensorimotor networks have been shown to develop around the third trimester of pregnancy ~30 wk (Thomason et al., 2015), while higher cognitive networks emerge later in neurodevelopment (Turk et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Higher cognitive networks emerge later in neurodevelopment than sensorimotor networks.
source: Sensorimotor networks have been shown to develop around the third trimester of pregnancy ~30 wk (Thomason et al., 2015), while higher cognitive networks emerge later in neurodevelopment (Turk et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The primitive form of the default mode network emerges around 35 wk in fetal or newborn rsfMRI.
source: For example, the primitive form of the default mode network emerges around 35 wk in fetal (Thomason et al., 2015; Thomason et al., 2014) or newborn (Doria et al., 2010) rsfMRI and highly resembles the adult configuration by the end of the first year (Gao et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The default mode network highly resembles the adult configuration by the end of the first year.
source: For example, the primitive form of the default mode network emerges around 35 wk in fetal (Thomason et al., 2015; Thomason et al., 2014) or newborn (Doria et al., 2010) rsfMRI and highly resembles the adult configuration by the end of the first year (Gao et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Analysis of fetal and neonatal rsfMRI data has heavily relied on linear models using heuristic knowledge learned from adult rsfMRI studies such as brain atlases, brain network patterns, or data-driven linear computational models such as independent component analysis (ICA).
source: However, to date, analysis of fetal and neonatal rsfMRI data has heavily relied on linear models, using heuristic knowledge learned from adult rsfMRI studies such as brain atlases (Turk et al., 2019), brain network patterns (Xu et al., 2019), or driven by data-driven linear computational models such as independent component analysis (ICA) (Eyre et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement describes the current state of the field and is supported by citations.

claim: In the regime of linear analytical models, complex rsfMRI data is considered as a linear combination of timeseries of several representations.
source: In the regime of linear analytical models, complex rsfMRI data (e.g., no. of vertex >50,000) is considered as a linear combination of timeseries of several representations (e.g., no. of cortical parcel = 360 or no. of IC components = 50–300).
evidence: This describes the mathematical framework of linear models.

claim: Modeling adult rsfMRI activity as a linear system has been shown to be a simple and reasonable approach.
source: While modeling adult rsfMRI activity as a linear system has been shown to be a simple and reasonable approach (Logothetis et al., 2001; Schölvinck et al., 2010; Mukamel et al., 2005) (see review Boynton et al., 2012), the utility of linear models in fetal– neonatal fMRI analysis can be limited due to the rapid neurodevelopment occurring during the fetal–neonatal stage (Andescavage et al., 2017; Clouchoux et al., 2012; Li et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The utility of linear models in fetal–neonatal fMRI analysis can be limited due to the rapid neurodevelopment occurring during the fetal–neonatal stage.
source: While modeling adult rsfMRI activity as a linear system has been shown to be a simple and reasonable approach (Logothetis et al., 2001; Schölvinck et al., 2010; Mukamel et al., 2005) (see review Boynton et al., 2012), the utility of linear models in fetal– neonatal fMRI analysis can be limited due to the rapid neurodevelopment occurring during the fetal–neonatal stage (Andescavage et al., 2017; Clouchoux et al., 2012; Li et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations about rapid neurodevelopment.

claim: The relation between hemodynamic function linking neural activity to the measured fMRI signal is nonlinear.
source: It is now recognized that the relation between hemodynamic function linking neural activity to the measured fMRI signal is nonlinear (Friston et al., 2000; Vazquez et al., 2006; Wager et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Recent studies with nonlinear modeling of fMRI data have yielded more informative brain representations compared to conventional linear methods, leading to significant improvements in disease classification.
source: Consequently, recent studies with nonlinear modeling of fMRI data have yielded more informative brain representations compared to conventional linear methods, leading to significant improvements in disease classification (Su et al., 2013) and identifying individual-specific (i.e., as opposed to group-averaged) brain features based on functional connectivity (FC) (Kim et al., 2021a), among others.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Nonlinear modeling of fMRI data has led to improvements in identifying individual-specific brain features based on functional connectivity (FC).
source: Consequently, recent studies with nonlinear modeling of fMRI data have yielded more informative brain representations compared to conventional linear methods, leading to significant improvements in disease classification (Su et al., 2013) and identifying individual-specific (i.e., as opposed to group-averaged) brain features based on functional connectivity (FC) (Kim et al., 2021a), among others.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Regions of the brain mature at different rates.
source: In addition to the nonlinearity inherent in fMRI measurement, studies have shown that regions of the brain mature at different rates (Doria et al., 2010; Eyre et al., 2021; Cao et al., 2017a).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Fetal inter-hemispheric long-range connectivity has an inflection point between 26 and 29 wk when connectivity strength rapidly increased in a region-specific manner (occipital before temporal before frontal region), and then plateaus at around 32 wk.
source: For example, fetal inter-hemispheric long-range connectivity has an inflection point between 26 and 29 wk when connectivity strength rapidly increased in a region-specific manner (i.e., occipital before temporal before frontal region), and then plateaus at around 32 wk (Jakab et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Investigation of fetal–neonatal FBNs using rsfMRI would likely require a computational approach that could potentially capture the nonlinearity inherent to rsfMRI data.
source: Taken together, these findings suggest that investigation of fetal–neonatal FBNs using rsfMRI would likely require a computational approach that could potentially capture the nonlinearity inherent to rsfMRI data into the model.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited findings about nonlinearity and differential maturation rates.

claim: Most investigations of emerging FC have utilized linear models, which may fail to capture important nonlinear information of the highly dynamic fetal–neonatal brain continuum.
source: To the best of our knowledge, most investigations of emerging FC have utilized linear models, which may fail to capture important nonlinear information of the highly dynamic fetal–neonatal brain continuum that is critical for more accurate characterization of functional brain development in the early stages of life.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of the field and a hypothesis about limitations of linear models.

claim: The authors developed a novel nonlinear analysis framework for adult rsfMRI using unsupervised deep generative model – variational autoencoder (VAE).
source: Recently, we developed a novel nonlinear analysis framework for adult rsfMRI using unsupervised deep generative model – variational autoencoder (VAE) (Kim et al., 2021a).
evidence: This describes prior work by the authors, supported by a citation.

claim: The VAE model learns a nonlinear feature set (or 'latent space') effectively using large-scale adult rsfMRI data through several nonlinear layers embedded in the VAE model.
source: Different from linear analytical models that decomposes complex, multivariate rs-fMRI data into independent, additive components, our VAE model learns a nonlinear feature set (or 'latent space') effectively using large-scale adult rsfMRI data through several nonlinear layers embedded in the VAE model.
evidence: This describes the methodology of the VAE model.

claim: The fully trained VAE model could disentangle generative factors of rsfMRI data and encode the learned representations as latent variables.
source: Our preliminary results in adults (Kim et al., 2021a) demonstrated that the fully trained VAE model could disentangle generative factors of rsfMRI data and encode the learned representations as latent variables.
evidence: This describes findings from prior work, supported by a citation.

claim: Generated VAE representations in the latent space were robust over varying signal quality of rsfMRI.
source: Noteworthy, generated VAE representations in the latent space were robust over varying signal quality of rsfMRI.
evidence: This describes a finding from prior work on VAE.

claim: The VAE could directly translate nonlinear information learnt from adult rsfMRI to nonlinearity of unseen fetal–neonatal rsfMRI.
source: Given the initial success, we posited that the VAE could directly translate nonlinear information learnt from adult rsfMRI to nonlinearity of unseen fetal–neonatal rsfMRI.
evidence: This is a hypothesis that motivated the current study.

claim: The authors hypothesized that nonlinear representations of fetal–neonatal rsfMRI, extracted using the VAE model pretrained with the rsfMRI of healthy adults, would carry more accurate and informative neural signatures of the prenatal-neonatal FBNs, compared to linear representations.
source: We hypothesized that nonlinear representations of fetal–neonatal rsfMRI, extracted using the VAE model pretrained with the rsfMRI of healthy adults, would carry more accurate and informative neural signatures of the prenatal-neonatal FBNs, compared to linear representations defined at the network scale using ICA or at the regional scale using multi-modal cortical parcel.
evidence: This is the main hypothesis of the study.

claim: The study conducted two experiments: compression of instantaneous fMRI patterns of subjects and prediction of gestational/postmenstrual ages (PMAs) using their rsfMRI scans.
source: To validate our hypothesis, we conducted two experiments: first, compression of instantaneous fMRI patterns of subjects; and second, prediction of gestational/postmenstrual ages (PMAs) using their rsfMRI scans.
evidence: This describes the experimental design of the study.

claim: The generalizability of findings was tested using two large datasets acquired by different institutions, together consisting of >500 fetuses, premature and healthy term-born neonates.
source: The generalizability of our findings was carefully tested using two large datasets acquired by different institutions, together consisting of >500 fetuses, premature and healthy term-born neonates.
evidence: This describes the datasets used in the study.

claim: Using latent variables at the group level, the authors mapped fetal–neonatal brain resting-state networks at different age groups.
source: Finally, using latent variables at the group level, we mapped fetal–neonatal brain resting-state networks at different age groups.
evidence: This describes an analysis performed in the study.

claim: The VAE model pretrained using adult rsfMRI data could extract meaningful representations of fetal–neonatal cortical activity.
source: We first determined whether our VAE model pretrained using adult rsfMRI data could extract meaningful representations of fetal–neonatal cortical activity.
evidence: This is a research question addressed in the study.

claim: The VAE model successfully reconstructed the fetal–neonatal cortical patterns but at the cost of some smoothing effects.
source: Qualitatively, we observed that the VAE model successfully reconstructed the fetal–neonatal cortical patterns but at the cost of some smoothing effects (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is a qualitative observation from the data shown in Figure 2.

claim: VAE showed more accurate reconstruction patterns compared to the original image, especially in the frontal and temporal regions, compared to linear latent spaces.
source: While linear latent spaces with different dimensions 50, 100, 200, and 300 (IC50-300) also exhibited reasonable reconstruction performance, VAE showed more accurate reconstruction patterns compared to the original image, especially in the frontal (Figure 2A) and temporal regions (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a finding from the data shown in Figure 2.

claim: VAE always showed the best spatial similarity compared to other linear counterparts across time points.
source: Although spatial similarity varied over time course, VAE always showed the best similarity compared to other linear counterparts.
evidence: This is a finding from the quantitative analysis of reconstruction performance.

claim: The observation that VAE showed superior reconstruction performance remained consistent at the group level and across different datasets.
source: This observation remained consistent at the group level and across different datasets (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a finding from the data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: IC maps with higher (=300) dimensions than VAE (=256) showed inferior reconstruction performance than VAE model.
source: Interestingly, IC maps with higher (=300) dimensions than VAE (=256) showed inferior reconstruction performance than VAE model (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a finding from the data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: MelodicIC (256 components) showed inferior reconstruction performance compared to the VAE or IC300.
source: To eliminate possible bias due to different number of components in the comparison, we derived IC map with 256 components (name as melodicIC) from the human adult rsfMRI data that was identically used in the VAE training and found that melodicIC showed inferior reconstruction performance compared to the VAE or IC300.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis comparing models with the same number of components.

claim: The difference in reconstruction performance between VAE and IC300 was statistically significant (paired t-test, Bonferroni-corrected p<10–3), for all datasets.
source: We further confirmed that the difference in reconstruction performance between VAE and IC300 was statistically significant (paired t-test, Bonferroni-corrected p<10–3), for all datasets.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the data analysis.

claim: The improved VAE reconstruction performance stemmed from its superior representations of neonatal rs-fcMRI, not merely from a stronger smoothing effect.
source: However, this was not observed, suggesting that the improved VAE reconstruction performance of the VAE stemmed from its superior representations of neonatal rs-fcMRI.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the smoothing analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: Reconstruction performance of adult rsfMRI was better than neonatal rsfMRI data.
source: As expected, reconstruction performance of adult rsfMRI (blue line) was better than neonatal rsfMRI data.
evidence: This is a finding from the smoothing analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: The maximum FWHM level was at 7 mm for adults compared to 5 mm for neonates.
source: Also, the maximum FWHM level was at 7 mm for adults compared to 5 mm for neonates.
evidence: This is a finding from the smoothing analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: The smoothing effect of the VAE is largely consistent against age-related characteristics of rsfMRI.
source: Given that brain size of newborns is about 60% of adults' brain size, this result suggested that smoothing effect of the VAE is largely consistent against age-related characteristics of rsfMRI.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the smoothing analysis.

claim: PMA at scan was significantly and positively correlated with the reconstruction performance for both dHCP (r = 0.20, p<0.01) and DBI (r = 0.35, p<0.01) datasets.
source: We found that PMA at scan was significantly and positively correlated with the reconstruction performance for both Developing Human Connectome Project (dHCP) (Figure 4A; r = 0.20, p<0.01) and Developing Brain Institute (DBI) (Figure 4B; r = 0.35, p<0.01) datasets.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The association between age at scan and reconstruction performance remained significant when only scans with good radiology scores were considered.
source: When only scans with good radiology scores (=1 or 1 + 2) were considered, the association between age at scan and reconstruction performance remained significant (group with radiology score = 1, normal appearance for age; n = 172, r = 0.19, p=0.01; score = 1 + 2, 2 = incidental findings with unlikely significance for clinical outcome or analysis; n = 292, r = 0.21, p<10–3).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from a subgroup analysis.

claim: For the fetal dataset, reconstruction performance was negatively correlated with GA (r = −0.69, p<10–4).
source: Conversely, for the fetal dataset, we found that the reconstruction performance was negatively correlated with GA (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C; r = −0.69, p<10–4).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the fetal data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The negative correlation between fetal age and reconstruction performance is in part due to the smoothing effect induced when registering the small size of the fetal brain to the standard 40 wk neonatal brain template.
source: We posit that this was in part due to the smoothing effect induced when registering the small size of the fetal brain (e.g., 19 wk) to the standard 40 wk neonatal brain template, for example, the brain size of fetus at GA = 19 wk was only 52 cc compared to 330 cc in fetus with GA = 32 wk (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a hypothesis to explain the negative correlation observed in fetal data.

claim: There was a strong negative association between brain size and reconstruction performance in fetuses.
source: Similarly, we observed a strong negative association between brain size and reconstruction performance (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is a finding from the fetal data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Once brain size was accounted for, the negative correlation between fetal age and reconstruction performance was reduced (r = −0.24, p=0.01).
source: Once brain size was accounted for, the negative correlation between age and reconstruction performance was reduced (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E, r = −0.24, p=0.01).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from a partial correlation analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Brain size in newborns was not significantly associated with reconstruction performance (r = 0.14, p=0.12).
source: In contrast, brain size in newborns was not significantly associated with reconstruction performance (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G, r = 0.14, p=0.12).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the neonatal data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1G.

claim: The positive age dependency of reconstruction performance in neonates remained significant even when considering brain size (r = 0.36, p<10–4).
source: Lastly, the positive age dependency of reconstruction performance in neonates remained significant even when considering brain size (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F, r = 0.36, p<10–4).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from a partial correlation analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F.

claim: In the dHCP dataset, reconstruction performance was negatively correlated with average frame-wise displacement level (r = −0.34, p<10–4).
source: In the dHCP dataset, reconstruction performance was negatively correlated with average frame-wise displacement level (r = −0.34, p<10–4) but not with brain size (r = −0.07, p=0.17).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the dHCP dataset.

claim: There was no significant correlation between PMA at scan and head motion in the dHCP dataset (r = 0.01, p=0.79).
source: There was no significant correlation between PMA at scan and head motion (r = 0.01, p=0.79).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the dHCP dataset.

claim: When head motion level was considered in the model, the age dependency of the reconstruction performance increased (r = 0.22, p<10–4).
source: When head motion level was considered in the model, the age dependency of the reconstruction performance increased (r = 0.22, p<10–4).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from a partial correlation analysis.

claim: After regressing out the age effect from the reconstruction performance, subjects having better reconstruction performance on their first scan also tended to have better reconstruction performance on their second scan in the dHCP dataset (r = 0.38, p<0.01; ICC = 0.38).
source: After regressing out the age effect from the reconstruction performance, we found that subjects having better reconstruction performance on their first scan also tended to have better reconstruction performance on their second scan (Figure 4E, left; r = 0.38, p<0.01; intraclass correlation coefficient [ICC] = 0.38).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the repeated scan analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: There was no significant correlation in the inter-session frame-wise head displacement in the dHCP dataset (r = 0.15, p=0.32).
source: We found that there was no significant correlation in the inter-session frame-wise head displacement (Figure 4—figure supplement 3, left; r = 0.15, p=0.32).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the repeated scan analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: The inter-session similarity of reconstruction performance remained significant after controlling for head motion (r = 0.30, p<0.05).
source: The inter-session similarity of reconstruction performance also remained significant after controlling for head motion (Figure 4—figure supplement 3, middle; r = 0.30, p<0.05).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from a partial correlation analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: The inter-session similarity of reconstruction performance was not driven by the variation in brain sizes for both dHCP and DBI datasets.
source: We further found the inter-session similarity of reconstruction performance was not driven by the variation in brain sizes for both dHCP and DBI datasets (for DBI dataset, Figure 4—figure supplement 1H; r = 0.36, p<0.01, and for dHCP dataset, Figure 4—figure supplement 3, middle; r = 0.37, p<0.01).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from partial correlation analyses shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1H and Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Individual variation of the reconstruction performance of resting-state fetal–neonatal brain activity was tightly connected not only to chronological brain maturity but also to the intrinsic neural traits of the subjects even during the in utero period.
source: Altogether, our results suggest that the individual variation of the reconstruction performance of resting-state fetal–neonatal brain activity was tightly connected not only to chronological brain maturity but also to the intrinsic neural traits of the subjects even during the in utero period.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the inter-session consistency findings.

claim: Latent variables derived by VAE yielded highly reliable age prediction accuracy in the dHCP dataset.
source: Through fusing tenfold cross-validation scheme and linear regression support vector machine (RSVM) in dHCP dataset, we found that latent variables derived by VAE yielded highly reliable prediction accuracy (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: This is a finding from the age prediction analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: The age prediction model with VAE-derived representations reached the best age prediction accuracy (RMSE = 1.98 ± 0.06, MAE = 1.53 ± 0.05, r2 = 0.72 ± 0.01) with a big margin compared to models based on linear latent features.
source: Interestingly, the age prediction model with VAE-derived representations reached the best age prediction accuracy; mean ± standard deviation over tenfolds, root mean squared error (RMSE) = 1.98 ± 0.06, mean absolute error (MAE) = 1.53 ± 0.05, r2 = 0.72 ± 0.01, with a big margin compared to models based on linear latent features (Table 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the age prediction analysis shown in Table 1.

claim: The percentage (=14.14 ± 0.32%) of VAE latent space representing age information was lower than most of the linear counterparts.
source: The percentage (=14.14 ± 0.32%) of latent space representing age information was lower than most of the linear counterparts (for cortical space, 76.53 ± 1.29%; for IC50, 44.84 ± 0.46%; for IC100, 32.55 ± 0.43%; for IC200, 16.07 ± 0.34%; for melodicIC, 29.97 ± 0.47%), except IC300 (=10.83 ± 0.25%).
evidence: This is a finding from the feature selection analysis in the age prediction task.

claim: The age prediction accuracy reached peak at melodicIC while accuracy deteriorated in the prediction model with features from 300 ICs (melodicIC: 1.76 ± 0.07 vs. 1.94 ± 0.07 for IC300).
source: It is noteworthy that different from the monotonic improvement of the reconstruction performance over increasing IC #, the age prediction accuracy reached peak at melodicIC while accuracy deteriorated in the prediction model with features from 300 ICs (melodicIC: 1.76 ± 0.07 vs. 1.94 ± 0.07 for IC300).
evidence: This is a finding from the age prediction analysis comparing different IC models.

claim: Nonlinear features extracted by VAE improved age prediction, outperforming linear features derived using ICA or cortical parcels.
source: Collectively, these results suggest that nonlinear features extracted by VAE improved age prediction, outperforming linear features derived using ICA or cortical parcels.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the age prediction results in Table 1.

claim: Latent variables derived by VAE reflected neurodevelopmental variability across fetuses and neonates more effectively than linear latent representations in the DBI dataset.
source: In line with findings in the dHCP dataset, the results clearly showed that latent variables derived by VAE reflected their neurodevelopmental variability across fetuses and neonates more effectively than linear latent representations (Table 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the age prediction analysis in the DBI dataset shown in Table 2.

claim: When the age prediction model considered a single age group (neonates or fetuses), the age prediction accuracy of VAE was superior to linear models only in neonates; cortical parcel showed better performance in fetuses.
source: When the age prediction model considered a single age group (neonates or fetuses), the age prediction accuracy of VAE was superior to linear models only in neonates; cortical parcel showed better performance in fetuses (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a finding from a subgroup analysis shown in Supplementary file 1.

claim: VAE showed the best cross-center prediction performance compared to linear models.
source: VAE showed the best cross-center prediction performance (Figure 6B) compared to linear models (Figure 6C and D).
evidence: This is a finding from the cross-center generalizability analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: VAE showed the least error (RMSE = 4.95 ± 0.66, MAE = 3.90 ± 0.65) in cross-center age prediction compared to other linear latent spaces.
source: Quantitatively, we confirmed our observation that VAE showed the least error (RMSE = 4.95 ± 0.66, MAE = 3.90 ± 0.65; n = 100 random trials with bootstrapping permutation method) compared to other linear latent spaces (Table 3); cortical parcel and IC maps showed comparable prediction performance.
evidence: This is a finding from the cross-center generalizability analysis shown in Table 3.

claim: Nonlinear latent representations featured by the VAE convey neural signatures reflecting brain maturity across a wide range of gestational and PMAs, in a more effective way than linear latent representations.
source: Altogether, these results strongly support our hypothesis that nonlinear latent representations featured by the VAE convey neural signatures reflecting brain maturity across a wide range of gestational and PMAs, in a more effective way than linear latent representations.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the age prediction and cross-center generalizability results.

claim: Each independent latent basis estimated from the neonate group exhibited a unique FBN pattern consisting of both activation and deactivation patterns.
source: Each independent latent basis estimated from the neonate group exhibited a unique FBN pattern consisting of both activation and deactivation patterns, as shown in Figure 7B.
evidence: This is a finding from the network mapping analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claim: IC8 in both the dHCP and DBI datasets showed activation/deactivation patterns between left and right early visual area.
source: For example, IC8 in both the dHCP and DBI datasets showed activation/deactivation patterns between left and right early visual area.
evidence: This is a specific finding from the network mapping analysis.

claim: Contrast between activation and deactivation was observed at the networks level: auditory vs. somatosensory (IC6 in dHCP; IC3 in DBI) and visual vs. auditory (IC3 in dHCP; IC4 in DBI).
source: This contrast (i.e., activation vs. deactivation) was also observed at the networks level; auditory vs. somatosensory (IC6 in dHCP; IC3 in DBI) and visual vs. auditory (IC3 in dHCP; IC4 in DBI).
evidence: This is a finding from the network mapping analysis.

claim: The neonatal auditory network having bilateral activation was identified in IC3 for both the dHCP and DBI dataset.
source: We also identified the neonatal auditory network having bilateral activation in IC3 for both the dHCP and DBI dataset.
evidence: This is a finding from the network mapping analysis.

claim: Precursors of the default mode network were observed (dHCP; IC29, DBI; IC21), which is coincident with findings in young adult rsfMRI studies.
source: Lastly, we observed precursors of the default mode network (dHCP; IC29, DBI; IC21; Figure 7B, right bottom), which is coincident with findings in young adult rsfMRI studies (Eyre et al., 2021; Van Essen et al., 2013; Gong et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a finding from the network mapping analysis, supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Inter-hemispheric opposition of the auditory network (IC22) was found in the dHCP dataset.
source: For example, we found inter-hemispheric opposition of the auditory network (IC22, Figure 7—figure supplement 1) and IC14 showed bilateral activation covering the higher visual network (Figure 7B, left bottom).
evidence: This is a finding from the network mapping analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: IC14 showed bilateral activation covering the higher visual network in the dHCP dataset.
source: For example, we found inter-hemispheric opposition of the auditory network (IC22, Figure 7—figure supplement 1) and IC14 showed bilateral activation covering the higher visual network (Figure 7B, left bottom).
evidence: This is a finding from the network mapping analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Global synchrony patterns, which are tightly related to global signal in fMRI data, were observed in the dHCP dataset (IC30) but not in the DBI dataset.
source: Global synchrony patterns, which are tightly related to global signal in fMRI data, were observed in the dHCP dataset (IC30, Figure 7—figure supplement 1), but not in the DBI dataset (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the network mapping analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1 and 2.

claim: In the DBI dataset, simultaneous activation of somatosensory, auditory, and visual networks with deactivation of temporoparietal junction was found (IC6).
source: In the DBI dataset, we found simultaneous activation of somatosensory, auditory, and visual networks with deactivation of temporoparietal junction that integrates sensory inputs (IC6, Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the network mapping analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: The best pattern similarity was achieved when ages were matched (full-term in dHCP vs. full-term in DBI), rather than between the age-unmatched groups from the same dataset.
source: The best pattern similarity was achieved when their ages were matched (black line; full-term in dHCP vs. full-term in DBI), rather than between the age-unmatched groups from the same dataset (red line: full-term vs. preterm in dHCP; blue line: full-term vs. fetus in DBI).
evidence: This is a finding from the network reproducibility analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The age-matched inter-dataset pattern similarity was higher than intra-dataset similarity with VAE-derived latent variables.
source: Specifically, the age-matched inter-dataset pattern similarity (black line in Figure 7C) was higher than intra-dataset similarity (red line in Figure 7C; full-term vs. preterm in dHCP) with VAE-derived latent variables.
evidence: This is a finding from the network reproducibility analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Linear models showed higher intra-dataset similarity than inter-dataset similarity, opposite to VAE.
source: Linear models, on the contrary, showed higher intra-dataset similarity (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is a finding from the network reproducibility analysis shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The VAE may be a better tool than linear models for capturing neurophysiologically relevant brain activity.
source: The finding that the VAE revealed similar network patterns in two independent, age-matched neonatal datasets suggests that the VAE may be a better tool than linear models for capturing neurophysiologically relevant brain activity.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the network reproducibility findings.

claim: ICA and cortical parcel techniques likely depended on features such as equivalent acquisition parameters, preprocessing, etc., that were similar between the pre- and full-term dHCP scans.
source: In contrast, it is likely that ICA and cortical parcel techniques depended on features such as equivalent acquisition parameters, preprocessing, etc., that were similar between the pre- and full-term dHCP scans.
evidence: This is a speculation to explain the difference in reproducibility between VAE and linear models.

claim: Of the 30 networks, the variance of 12 networks (IC2, 3, 6, 7, 10, 11, 16, 20, 21, 24, 25, 26, and 27) was significantly correlated with PMA at scan (FDR-corrected p<0.05).
source: Of the 30 networks, the variance of 12 networks (IC2, 3, 6, 7, 10, 11, 16, 20, 21, 24, 25, 26, and 27) was significantly correlated with PMA at scan (FDR-corrected p<0.05; r = 0.22, 0.29, 0.15,–0.16, –0.31, 0.16, 0.14, 0.17, 0.27, 0.16, 0.19, and 0.17, respectively).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the age-related network analysis.

claim: IC6, the component most strongly correlated with PMA (r = 0.29, FDR-corrected p<10–6), highlighted the joint of two networks, auditory and somatosensory.
source: Among 12 functional networks, we further explored the age-dependent changes in IC6, the component most strongly correlated with PMA (Figure 8C; r = 0.29, FDR-corrected p<10–6). IC6 highlighted the joint of two networks, auditory and somatosensory; activation in somatosensory with deactivation in auditory (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is a finding from the age-related network analysis shown in Figure 8.

claim: Old group showed higher variance than younger group at IC6 (uncorrected p<10–7).
source: As suggested by the correlational analysis, old group showed higher variance than younger group at IC6 (Figure 8D; uncorrected p<10–7; see Figure 8—figure supplement 1 for other networks) suggesting evolution of neonatal FBNs over aging.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the age group comparison shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Compared to the young group, the old group showed mildly stronger activation in the somatosensory region, stronger activation in the posterior insular region extending to the primary auditory region, and weaker activation in the superior temporal auditory region.
source: For example, compared to the young group, the old group showed (1) mildly stronger activation in the somatosensory region, (2) stronger activation in the posterior insular region extending to the primary auditory region, and (3) weaker activation in the superior temporal auditory region (highlighted by black arrows in Figure 8E).
evidence: This is a qualitative finding from the age group comparison shown in Figure 8E.

claim: Functional networks of older groups showed stronger engagement of primary auditory area, with some level of lateralization toward the right hemisphere.
source: Functional networks of older groups showed stronger engagement of primary auditory area, with some level of lateralization toward the right hemisphere; no change in somatosensory region was observed.
evidence: This is a finding from the age group comparison in latent space shown in Figure 8F.

claim: The brain network engages additional brain region with advancing age (or maturity), suggesting the recharacterization of brain systems in the first weeks of the postnatal period.
source: To summarize, our results demonstrate that the brain network engages additional brain region with advancing age (or maturity), suggesting the recharacterization of brain systems in the first weeks of the postnatal period.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the age-related network findings.

claim: VAE showed better reconstruction performance of fMRI patterns compared to ICA for each subject and across different age groups.
source: In this study, VAE showed better reconstruction performance of fMRI patterns compared to ICA for each subject and across different age groups (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the reconstruction performance analysis.

claim: VAE outperformed ICA age prediction even when the dimensions of ICA (=300) latent variables exceeded that of the VAE (=256).
source: Interestingly, VAE outperformed ICA age prediction even when the dimensions of ICA (=300) latent variables exceeded that of the VAE (=256).
evidence: This is a finding from the age prediction analysis.

claim: The nonlinear nature of deep convolutional models is a key for the model to extract meaningful features against morphological bias/changes of objects.
source: In the computer vision field, deep learning studies Russakovsky et al., 2015; Krizhevsky et al., 2012 have suggested that the nonlinear nature of deep convolutional models is a key for the model to extract meaningful features against morphological bias/changes of objects, for example, shift, rotation, or magnification in the image, yielding superior image classification performance.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work in computer vision.

claim: The percentage of VAE-derived latent variables sensitive to age prediction in dHCP dataset was comparable to the one observed in the DBI dataset (14.14 ± 0.32 vs. 11.39 ± 0.35%).
source: Supporting this notion, we found that the percentage of VAE-derived latent variables sensitive to age prediction in dHCP dataset was comparable to the one observed in the DBI dataset (14.14 ± 0.32 vs. 11.39 ± 0.35%, for dHCP and DBI), whereas larger inter-dataset discrepancies were observed with linear models (most difference was in cortical parcel; 76.53 ± 1.29 vs. 11.39 ± 0.35% and least difference was in the IC300; 10.83 ± 0.25 vs. 5.24 ± 0.23%, for dHCP and DBI).
evidence: This is a finding from the feature selection analysis comparing datasets.

claim: A cascade of nonlinear operations, efficiently implemented through several layers in the VAE architecture, disentangles complex brain activity patterns from residual nonlinear noise or artifact.
source: Collectively, we posit that a cascade of nonlinear operations, efficiently implemented through several layers in our designed VAE architecture, disentangles complex brain activity patterns from residual nonlinear noise or artifact, differentiating the VAE model from linear models such as cortical parcel or ICA.
evidence: This is a hypothesis to explain the superior performance of VAE.

claim: FC patterns in individuals carry distinct signatures that are distinguishable from others.
source: Recent neuroimaging studies have shown that FC patterns in individuals carry distinct signatures that are distinguishable from others (Horien et al., 2019; Finn et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Unique FC patterns remained stable over time for about 3 years in adults.
source: This unique pattern, according to a recent study, remained stable over time for about 3 years (Horien et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: One neonatal study showed nearly no self-similarity of FC patterns between repeated scans (=11%).
source: One neonatal study (Ciarrusta et al., 2021) that explored individual uniqueness of brain FC pattern by identifying individuals based on their FC profiles showed nearly no self-similarity of FC patterns between repeated scans (=11%) (Ciarrusta et al., 2021), suggesting that the functional uniqueness of the human brain likely emerges after the newborn period.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Another study suggested that individual uniqueness was already apparent during the newborn period reaching an accuracy of 100% (n = 40).
source: In contrast, another study suggested that individual uniqueness was already apparent during the newborn period reaching an accuracy of 100% (n = 40) (Wang et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The perfect accuracy in Wang et al. 2021 was likely largely driven by measurement artifact.
source: Thus, the perfect accuracy was likely largely driven by measurement artifact as suggested in King et al., 2023.
evidence: This is an inference supported by a citation.

claim: Adults (~92%) showed higher inter-scan similarity than newborns.
source: Compared to newborn data Ciarrusta et al., 2021, adults (~92%) Finn et al., 2015, children/youth (6–21 years old, ~43%) Horien et al., 2019, and infants (~1 year old,~70%) Hu et al., 2022 showed higher inter-scan similarity.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Significant self-similarity was observed between repeated ex utero scans (r = 0.38) and longitudinal in utero and ex utero scans (r = 0.39).
source: In keeping with these data, we observed significant self-similarity – defined as the degree of similarity of reconstructed brain data – between repeated ex utero scans (r = 0.38, Figure 4E, left) and longitudinal in utero and ex utero scans (r = 0.39, Figure 4E, right).
evidence: This is a finding from the inter-session similarity analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Lower (or higher) reconstruction performance in fetuses or neonates can be interpreted as lower (or higher) similarity of their FC representations to the adult brain.
source: As the VAE was trained to represent resting-state brain activity of neurotypical adults, lower (or higher) reconstruction performance in fetuses or neonates can be interpreted as lower (or higher) similarity of their FC representations to the adult brain.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the reconstruction performance findings.

claim: The age dependency of reconstruction performance could be interpreted as errors introduced when projecting fMRI in individual brain space into the 40 wk standard brain template.
source: It is possible that errors were introduced when projecting fMRI in individual brain space into the 40 wk standard brain template.
evidence: This is an alternative interpretation of the age dependency findings.

claim: The error induced by geometric reformatting was minimal (r ~ 0.98 between the original cortical pattern and reformatted/recovered cortical pattern) in adults.
source: We believe that this was unlikely, given that in our previous experiment with human adults (see Supplementary Figure 1 in Kim et al., 2021a), we showed that the error induced by geometric reformatting was minimal (r ~ 0.98 between the original cortical pattern and reformatted/recovered cortical pattern).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Learned generative factors (latent variables) in the VAE largely fall into two groups: one representing the common pattern of brain dynamics and the other shaping the unique brain patterns of individuals.
source: In adults Kim et al., 2021a, we hypothesized that our trained VAE model was able to extract generative factors of rsfMRI data as a form of latent variable. In the VAE, we speculated that learned generative factors, that is, latent variables, largely fall into two groups: one representing the common pattern of brain dynamics and the other shaping the unique brain patterns of individuals.
evidence: This is a hypothesis from prior work.

claim: A subset of latent variables of fetal–neonatal rsfMRI mapped to a set of large-scale FBNs (visual, auditory, sensorimotor, and default mode network).
source: Supporting this notion, in this study, we observed that a subset of latent variables of fetal–neonatal rsfMRI mapped to a set of large-scale FBNs, for example, visual, auditory, and sensorimotor, and default mode network (Figure 7, Figure 7—figure supplements 1 and 2), whereas another subset reflected the temporal properties of fetal–neonatal functional brain development (Figures 5 and 6, Tables 1–3).
evidence: This is a finding from the network mapping and age prediction analyses.

claim: Another subset of latent variables reflected the temporal properties of fetal–neonatal functional brain development.
source: Supporting this notion, in this study, we observed that a subset of latent variables of fetal–neonatal rsfMRI mapped to a set of large-scale FBNs, for example, visual, auditory, and sensorimotor, and default mode network (Figure 7, Figure 7—figure supplements 1 and 2), whereas another subset reflected the temporal properties of fetal–neonatal functional brain development (Figures 5 and 6, Tables 1–3).
evidence: This is a finding from the age prediction analyses.

claim: Some subsets of latent variables (large-scale FBNs) varied with advancing PMA.
source: Additionally, we found that some subsets of latent variables (i.e., large-scale FBNs) varied with advancing PMA.
evidence: This is a finding from the age-related network analysis.

claim: The brain network (IC6) characterized by additional engagement of primary auditory network when neonatal brain matured.
source: For example, the brain network (IC6), which showed joint highlights in somatosensory and auditory brain regions, characterized by additional engagement of primary auditory network when neonatal brain matured.
evidence: This is a finding from the age-related network analysis of IC6.

claim: Spatial involving nature of neurodevelopment pattern during neonatal period is largely in line with the trend in maturing brain system at older age that transit from 'segregation' into 'integration'.
source: Spatial involving nature of neurodevelopment pattern during neonatal period, observed in our study, is largely in line with the trend in maturing brain system at older age that transit from 'segregation' into 'integration,' suggested by other studies (Fair et al., 2009; Dosenbach et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The VAE can identify spatial aspect of neurodevelopment during perinatal period, which are difficult to be achieved by conventional linear counterparts.
source: Altogether, our results highlight that the VAE can identify spatial aspect of neurodevelopment during perinatal period, which are difficult to be achieved by conventional linear counterparts.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the age-related network findings.

claim: The delineation of generative factors of fetal–neonatal rsfMRI is plausible using the VAE model pretrained on adult rsfMRI without any further introduction of new fetal–neonatal fMRI data to the VAE training.
source: Nonetheless, our findings suggest the delineation of generative factors of fetal–neonatal rsfMRI is plausible using the VAE model pretrained on adult rsfMRI without any further introduction of new fetal–neonatal fMRI data to the VAE training.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the overall findings.

claim: VAE may be used to create longitudinal maps of the functional brain connectome throughout the life span (i.e., a functional atlas from the fetal period to adulthood).
source: Collectively, we believe that VAE may be used to create longitudinal maps of the functional brain connectome throughout the life span (i.e., a functional atlas from the fetal period to adulthood).
evidence: This is a speculation about future applications of VAE.

claim: Latent features of fetal–neonatal rsfMRI likely reflect both 'real' aspects of the fetal–neonatal functional connectome and similarity/dissimilarity to the adult functional connectome.
source: Our results suggest that both aspects are likely captured by latent features; some fundamental functional networks that remain largely consistent over neonatal period, reflecting the actual aspect of fetal–neonatal functional connectome. In contrast, some networks evolved over time (e.g., IC 6 in Figure 8); thus, some portions of their latent features may be driven by the dissimilarity/similarity to the adult network.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the network mapping findings.

claim: Brain networks reported in this study exhibited more dynamic patterns such as lateralized activation, bilateral activation, activation and deactivation across hemisphere, and interaction between brain networks compared to FBNs defined by spatial ICA on the dHCP dataset.
source: Compared to FBNs defined by spatial ICA on the dHCP dataset (Eyre et al., 2021), brain networks reported in our study exhibited more dynamic patterns such as lateralized activation, bilateral activation, activation and deactivation across hemisphere, and interaction between brain networks (Figure 7, Figure 7—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is a comparison of findings to prior work.

claim: The discrepancy in FBN patterns mainly originates from the methodological difference between temporal and spatial ICA.
source: We believe the discrepancy in FBN patterns mainly originates from the methodological difference between temporal and spatial ICA.
evidence: This is a hypothesis to explain differences in findings.

claim: Temporal ICA outputs temporally independent functional modes having activation patterns along with deactivation patterns.
source: As shown in previous studies with adults (Smith et al., 2012), different from spatial ICA, temporal ICA outputs temporally independent functional modes having activation patterns along with deactivation patterns.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Opposition between sensory-related networks was observed (#4: auditory vs. somatosensory; #16: visual vs. auditory).
source: Similarly, we also observed the opposition between sensory-related networks (#4: auditory vs. somatosensory; #16: visual vs. auditory, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the network mapping analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Anticorrelated activity between cognitive networks and sensory networks was not observed in neonates, possibly suggesting such suppression of sensory functions via higher cognitive networks develops at a later neurodevelopmental phase.
source: However, unlike the adult brain, we were not able to observe anticorrelated activity between cognitive networks and sensory networks, possibly suggesting such suppression of sensory functions via higher cognitive networks develops at a later neurodevelopmental phase.
evidence: This is an observation and speculation about developmental differences.

claim: The smoothing effect of the VAE was comparable to IC300 (similar effect to manual smoothing at the level of FWHM = 5 mm).
source: Another interesting observation was that the smoothing effect of the VAE was comparable to IC300 (similar effect to manual smoothing at the level of FWHM = 5 mm; Figure 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the smoothing analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: The VAE model may be more suitable for investigating finer scale of brain networks than linear models.
source: Given the above, we believe the VAE model may be more suitable for investigating finer scale of brain networks than linear models.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the smoothing analysis findings.

claim: The VAE model with a greater number of latent variables (e.g., 512 or 1024 instead of 256) can be utilized to find brain networks at finer scale.
source: Perhaps, the VAE model with a greater number of latent variables (e.g., 512 or 1024 instead of 256 in the current VAE) can be utilized to find brain networks at finer scale.
evidence: This is a speculation about future applications of VAE.

claim: The proposed analysis scheme combining nonlinear spatial compression via VAE and temporal modeling via temporal ICA may be a critical addition to existing tools for mapping fetal–neonatal brain networks.
source: Altogether, we expect our proposed analysis scheme combining nonlinear spatial compression via VAE and temporal modeling via temporal ICA may be a critical addition to existing tools for mapping fetal–neonatal brain networks.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the potential impact of the method.

claim: FBNs identified in the DBI dataset were relatively less straightforward to interpret compared to the dHCP dataset, possibly due to smaller scan size, shorter data length, different preprocessing steps such as ICA-FIX, or a combination of the above.
source: In general, we observed that FBNs identified in the DBI dataset were relatively less straightforward to interpret compared to the dHCP dataset, possibly due to many factors including, but not limited to, smaller scan size, shorter data length, different preprocessing steps such as ICA-FIX, or a combination of the above (see Figure 7—figure supplements 1 and 2 for the whole set of FBNs from dHCP and DBI datasets, respectively).
evidence: This is an observation and speculation about dataset differences.

claim: FBNs defined by the linear models (IC50, IC200, and IC300) were more sensitive to inter-dataset difference, resulting in lesser pattern similarity between dHCP and DBI full-term groups, and greater similarity between pre- and full-term newborns within the dHCP dataset.
source: Related, we found that FBNs defined by the linear models (IC50, IC200, and IC300) were more sensitive to inter-dataset difference, resulting in lesser pattern similarity between dHCP and DBI full-term groups, and greater similarity between pre- and full-term newborns within the dHCP dataset (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is a finding from the network reproducibility analysis shown in Figure 7D.

claim: 30 FBNs derived by VAE were more replicable across different datasets when their ages were matched.
source: Opposite to linear models, we found that 30 FBNs derived by FBNs were more replicable across different datasets when their ages were matched.
evidence: This is a finding from the network reproducibility analysis.

claim: The VAE model can be an analysis tool for big fMRI data collected throughout multiple centers.
source: Collectively, we believe that the VAE model can be an analysis tool for big fMRI data collected throughout multiple centers.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the potential application of VAE.

claim: One limitation is that the VAE model primarily focused on learning spatial representations of rsfMRI patterns and ignored the temporal dynamics of rsfMRI data.
source: While the VAE model was able to represent fetal–neonatal FC data, one limitation is that the model primarily focused on learning spatial representations of rsfMRI patterns and ignored the temporal dynamics of rsfMRI data.
evidence: This is a stated limitation of the current VAE model.

claim: Functional MRI is not stationary.
source: Functional MRI is not stationary (Guan et al., 2020), and our future work aims to address both spatial and temporal features of rsfMRI; currently, limitations on technical resources constrained our ability to simultaneously model both.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Another limitation relates to the smoothing effect induced by the VAE which could render it insensitive to detecting fine-grained changes of early network development.
source: Another limitation of our study relates to the smoothing effect induced by the VAE which could render it insensitive to detecting fine-grained changes of early network development.
evidence: This is a stated limitation of the VAE model.

claim: The VAE model does exert some level of smoothing when mapping latent variables to the cortical space.
source: As observed in Figures 2 and 3, the VAE model does exert some level of smoothing when mapping latent variables to the cortical space.
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: The VAE outperforms linear models given the same degree of smoothing.
source: It should be noted too that the VAE outperforms linear models given the same degree of smoothing.
evidence: This is a finding from the smoothing analysis.

claim: Another limitation is that the VAE model currently does not capture information from the subcortex.
source: Another limitation is that our VAE model currently does not capture information from the subcortex.
evidence: This is a stated limitation of the current VAE model.

claim: The subcortex plays a critical role in neural circuitry formation.
source: This region plays a critical role in neural circuitry formation and including subcortical neural activity in future studies would greatly enhance our understanding of the developing functional connectome (Fransson et al., 2009; Lordier et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The current VAE model was pretrained on adult rsfMRI data.
source: Lastly, the current VAE model was pretrained on adult rsfMRI data.
evidence: This describes a characteristic of the current VAE model.

claim: Future studies incorporating newborn rsfMRI data would likely help emphasize features uniquely present in the developing brain.
source: Future studies incorporating newborn rsfMRI data would likely help emphasize features uniquely present in the developing brain.
evidence: This is a speculation about future improvements to the VAE model.

claim: The study applied a novel deep generative model to a large (>500) fetal–neonatal rsfMRI dataset to extract nonlinear brain representations of healthy fetuses, preterm neonates, and full-term infants.
source: In this study, we applied a novel deep generative model to a large (>500) fetal–neonatal rsfMRI dataset to extract nonlinear brain representations of healthy fetuses, preterm neonates, and full-term infants.
evidence: This summarizes the main contribution of the study.

claim: The pretrained adult VAE model was applicable to fetal–neonatal rsfMRI data, but there is room for improvement.
source: Our results suggest that the pretrained adult VAE model was applicable to fetal–neonatal rsfMRI data, but there is room for improvement.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the applicability of the VAE model.

claim: Fine-tuning the VAE with fetal–neonatal rsfMRI will help the VAE to learn more meaningful network representations.
source: First, we expect that fine-tuning the VAE with fetal–neonatal rsfMRI will help the VAE to learn more meaningful network representations.
evidence: This is a speculation about future improvements to the VAE model.

claim: The beta hyperparameter in the current model was set to 9, putting more weight on the usefulness of learned latent variables.
source: In the current model, the beta hyperparameter, which balances reconstruction performance and usefulness of learned latent variables, was set to 9, putting more weight on the latter term.
evidence: This describes a hyperparameter setting in the VAE model.

claim: Changing the setting of beta value to meet the specific goals of other studies will be of great important in future VAE applications for fetal–neonatal rsfMRI.
source: Changing the setting of beta value to meet the specific goals of other studies will be of great important in future VAE applications for fetal–neonatal rsfMRI.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future applications of VAE.

claim: A promising application of the VAE model may be for characterizing the developing brain's functional connectome.
source: A promising application of the VAE model may be for characterizing the developing brain's functional connectome.
evidence: This is a speculation about future applications of VAE.

claim: It has been suggested that a nascent default mode network (DMN) exists in fetuses.
source: For example, it has been suggested that a nascent default mode network (DMN) exists in fetuses (Thomason et al., 2015), while the DMN of neonates has been shown to closely resemble the human adult (Doria et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The DMN of neonates has been shown to closely resemble the human adult.
source: For example, it has been suggested that a nascent default mode network (DMN) exists in fetuses (Thomason et al., 2015), while the DMN of neonates has been shown to closely resemble the human adult (Doria et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Due to the linear nature of conventional models such as ICA, it is difficult to capture the spatial evolution of FBNs over aging.
source: However, due to the linear nature of conventional models such as ICA, it is difficult to capture the spatial evolution of FBNs over aging.
evidence: This is a statement about limitations of linear models.

claim: Linear ICA can show changes in network strength but not changes in network spatial patterns with aging.
source: For example, linear ICA can show changes in network strength but not changes in network spatial patterns with aging (see Figure 4 in Eyre et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The VAE model is nonlinear such that combining two latent variables in the latent space can yield continuous change of network patterns in the cortical space.
source: In contrast, the VAE model is nonlinear such that combining two latent variables in the latent space can yield continuous change of network patterns in the cortical space (i.e., adding/subtracting age-related latent variable from DMN-related latent variable and projecting into the cortical space using the VAE decoder).
evidence: This describes a capability of the VAE model.

claim: Findings showing a difference in age group-wise network patterns between latent vs. cortical spaces suggested the possibility of mapping strategy that can track the neurodevelopmental growth of fetal–neonatal FBNs.
source: Related to it, our findings showing a difference in age group-wise network patterns between latent vs. cortical spaces (Figure 8—figure supplement 2) suggested the possibility of the above mapping strategy that can track the neurodevelopmental growth of fetal–neonatal FBNs.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the findings shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claim: The VAE model may provide important insights into fetal–neonatal neurodevelopmental growth trajectories.
source: Thus, the VAE model may provide important insights into fetal–neonatal neurodevelopmental growth trajectories.
evidence: This is a speculation about the potential impact of VAE.

claim: New insights regarding the complex nonlinear brain development that occurs during the prenatal-neonatal continuum may allow us to identify early biomarkers for neurobehavioral vulnerability.
source: New insights regarding the complex nonlinear brain development that occurs during the prenatal-neonatal continuum may allow us to identify early biomarkers for neurobehavioral vulnerability and link specific prenatal brain developmental processes associated with aberrant neural connectivity which may underlie prevalent child and adult neurological disorders.
evidence: This is a speculation about the potential clinical impact of the research.

claim: The study analyzed 270 resting-state scans from 95 healthy fetuses and 160 full-term-born healthy infants from the DBI dataset.
source: We analyzed 270 resting-state scans from 95 healthy fetuses and 160 full-term-born healthy infants.
evidence: This describes the sample size of the DBI dataset.

claim: Fetuses in the DBI dataset were scanned between 19.14 and 39.71 gestational weeks (mean and SD; 33.65 ± 4.01).
source: Fetuses (49 females) from healthy pregnancies were scanned between 19.14 and 39.71 gestational weeks (mean and SD; 33.65 ± 4.01).
evidence: This describes the age range of fetuses in the DBI dataset.
